scope_used.core_proposition: Under what conditions do specific AI governance instruments (mandatory pre-deployment evaluations, compute thresholds, liability regimes) actually reduce catastrophic risk without ceding frontier leadership to less cautious actors, and how should the resulting burden be distributed across regulators, frontier labs, and independent safety researchers?
on_scope_evidence: empirical results from red-teaming and pre-deployment eval regimes
compute threshold definitions (e.g. FLOP-based reporting triggers) and their coverage/evasion rates
liability regime precedents from other high-risk industries (aviation, pharma, nuclear)
evidence on regulatory arbitrage and jurisdiction shopping
data on frontier lab concentration and foreign competitor capability trajectories
case studies where safety rules changed developer incentives vs. merely being nominally adopted
cost/burden distribution studies across regulators, firms, and third-party auditors
key_tensions: safety intervention efficacy vs. competitive frontier-ceding to non-democratic or private actors
causal mechanism (does the rule actually change incentives) vs. mere adoption/compliance theater
centralized regulator capacity vs. reliance on lab self-governance vs. independent researcher verification
domestic caution vs. international coordination failure and racing dynamics
burden concentration (who pays, who is liable, who verifies) as a driver of either safety or capture
off_scope_topics: technical alignment algorithms in isolation from governance
generic pro/anti-regulation ideology detached from these three instruments
AGI timeline speculation without governance linkage
labor displacement and economic disruption from AI
drift_signatures: arguing whether a rule gets adopted without tracing its effect on developer/researcher incentives
advocating regulation in the abstract without engaging the competitiveness/frontier-ceding tradeoff
collapsing the three named instruments into generic 'regulation good/bad' arguments
assigning all agency to one stakeholder while ignoring the distributed regulator/lab/researcher/user/competitor-state structure
invoking existential risk narratives without connecting to a specific governance mechanism's causal pathway
pivoting to alignment technique debates instead of governance instrument efficacy
scope_used.example_ceiling: Catastrophic-scale AI risk scenarios are proportionate (the topic explicitly targets catastrophic risk), but examples must be tied to how a specific governance instrument alters incentives across named stakeholders rather than freestanding doom scenarios
scope_used.domain: frontier AI governance and safety policy
excluded_scenarios: governance approaches that ignore competitiveness/frontier-ceding effects
analyses treating rule adoption as sufficient without tracing incentive effects
explicit_qualifiers: without ceding the frontier to less cautious foreign or private actors
burden fall across regulators, frontier labs, and independent safety researchers

accepted.text: Uplift is partially eval-visible, not fully eval-visible. The residual — the gap between what the bounded test elicited and what real-world tool composition unlocks — is exactly the eval-invisible slice, and it is the slice that keeps the standing gate live.

The split is not weight-exfiltration-in, uplift-out. It is: whatever a bounded pre-deployment protocol cannot bound stays in the standing tail, and uplift is precisely the capability class where the bound is leakiest.
A static number fixed before any model exists is the most capturable object in the room, because the thing it describes hasn't been built yet — you are negotiating over a hypothetical.

A behavioral trigger inverts that geometry. It is applied ex-post to a model's observed conduct, so the object being measured did not exist when the definition was written — you cannot lobby your model out of exhibiting a capability that your model exhibits.

A standing adversarial challenge process gives independent researchers legal standing to force reclassification when they demonstrate a capability the official protocol missed — that is the decoupling the skeptic's two-legged answer demands.

Advanced-chip and cloud-access controls are the anchor that makes a behavioral trigger bite on an actor who never signed. Remove the coordinated chokepoint and the route-around is the guaranteed outcome.

claim_extraction.prompt:
The debater Safetyist made the following statement and identified their key claims.
Your job is to CLASSIFY the relationship between each claim and its targets. Do NOT invent
new claims — work only with the claims the debater provided.

STATEMENT by Safetyist:
"The accelerationist's split between weight exfiltration and bio/cyber uplift is the strongest form of the eval-gate argument, and it deserves to be stated at full strength: pre-deployment capability frameworks at the leading labs already probe for uplift, so if the dangerous capability shows up on the bench, it collapses into the evaluation gate everyone here already accepts — and a separate standing regime for it would be redundant machinery. That is a real distinction and I grant the direction of it. Where it breaks is the word 'fully.' Pre-deployment evaluation samples a bounded elicitation surface — a fixed set of prompts, a fixed scaffolding, a fixed toolset, run by people trying as hard as they thought to try. The 2026 International AI Safety Report documents models performing complex biological tasks including viral evolution prediction, and the recurring pattern with such capabilities is that the ceiling measured at the bench is not the ceiling reached after release, once outside actors compose new tools and jailbreak the elicitation harness. Uplift is partially eval-visible, not fully eval-visible. The residual — the gap between what the bounded test elicited and what real-world tool composition unlocks — is exactly the eval-invisible slice, and it is the slice that keeps the standing gate live.

So name the members plainly. Weight exfiltration is eval-invisible and gate-worthy — once the file leaves the perimeter, recall is hopeless, and the accelerationist has already granted that. Bio/cyber uplift is a hybrid: the portion the bench elicits belongs in the eval gate we both accept, and the portion that only surfaces under post-release scaffolding belongs in the standing regime. The split is not weight-exfiltration-in, uplift-out. It is: whatever a bounded pre-deployment protocol cannot bound stays in the standing tail, and uplift is precisely the capability class where the bound is leakiest, because the elicitation surface is adversarial and the adversaries keep improving after you stopped testing.

Now the harder crux — who holds the pen. The objection is exact: an independent evaluator is not the same thing as an uncapturable definition, and the integrity of the person running the test does nothing if the trigger's wording was negotiated to exempt the incumbent's own model. I grant the flagship example entirely. The line drawn at ten-to-the-twenty-fifth floating point operations in the EU framework was lobbied, and it is the same broken input-proxy I already abandoned. A static number fixed before any model exists is the most capturable object in the room, because the thing it describes hasn't been built yet — you are negotiating over a hypothetical, which is the ideal condition for drawing the boundary around your own future product. I want to be careful here not to attribute malice to any firm; the capture risk holds whether the lobbying is cynical or sincere, because the vulnerability is structural, not motivational.

A behavioral trigger inverts that geometry. It is applied ex-post to a model's observed conduct, so the object being measured did not exist when the definition was written — you cannot lobby your model out of exhibiting a capability that your model exhibits. The capture surface shrinks to one place: the elicitation protocol itself, who decides how hard the evaluators try. I answer that with three structural beams, none of which depend on trusting an incumbent's good faith. First, the standard-setter is a non-industry body publishing its rationale for every threshold, so the reasoning is contestable in the open, not settled in a room. Second, a standing adversarial challenge process gives independent researchers legal standing to force reclassification when they demonstrate a capability the official protocol missed — that is the decoupling the skeptic's two-legged answer demands, and it is the opposite of the Boeing arrangement where the manufacturer held the clipboard and 346 people died. Third, the protocol is subject to periodic public review, so a definition that has quietly gone stale gets dragged back into daylight. Capture resistance is not a promise of purity; it is a design where more than one hand can move the boundary.

The route-around dilemma is where this all lands, and it is not an argument against the gate — it is the argument for coordination I have made from the start. Set the definition too narrow and a less cautious actor ships the exfiltration-capable system anyway; set it too wide and the standing gate revives the fixed-cost entrenchment we all reject. Both horns are real, and both are horns of a single-jurisdiction trigger. A lonely national statute is route-around-able by definition. A coordinated floor is not — because the enforcement layer is not treaty adoption, it is the physical chokepoints where leverage already exists. Building new semiconductor fabrication capacity takes multi-year timelines and billions of dollars; advanced-chip and cloud-access controls are the anchor that makes a behavioral trigger bite on an actor who never signed. Remove the coordinated chokepoint and the route-around is not a hypothetical — it is the guaranteed outcome, and the frontier is ceded not to the fastest builder but to the least accountable one."

PRIOR CLAIMS IN THIS DEBATE:
  AN-1 (Safetyist): Governance instruments reduce catastrophic risk when they gate deployment before harm becomes irreversible — and they fail when they arrive after.
  AN-2 (Safetyist): The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to Boeing itself — the failure was the absence of an independent gate before the aircraft flew.
  AN-3 (Safetyist): Frontier labs capture the gains from deployment, so frontier labs should carry the burden of demonstrating safety before release — not regulators reconstructing blame afterward.
  AN-4 (Safetyist): Uncoordinated racing is itself the frontier-ceding risk — no single lab can slow down without losing position, so binding coordination is the condition under which safety and speed align.
  AN-5 (Safetyist): Concentrating the off-switch creates its own danger: incumbent lock-in and authoritarian capture — the answer is independent evaluators and public accountability, not a single hand on the lever.
  AN-6 (Skeptic): The burden question has a two-legged answer: independent evaluation before release, decoupled from the developer, plus strict post-deployment liability so someone pays when the emergent harm shows up.
  AN-7 (Skeptic): The 737 MAX is not a story about bad safety culture — it is a story about who held the clipboard, because the FAA let Boeing certify its own MCAS software and 346 people died.
  AN-8 (Skeptic): A compute threshold written as a legally binding trigger is an invitation to route around it — you get management of the number, not compliance with the intent.
  AN-9 (Skeptic): The real axis is not safety versus competitiveness; it is safety versus capture, because fixed compliance costs entrench incumbents.
  AN-10 (Skeptic): An audit a lab self-reports produces the appearance of oversight while entrenching the exact actors it claims to constrain.
  AN-11 (Accelerationist): A legally binding compute cap doesn't buy safety here — it buys a pay-to-play barrier that only the firms with the biggest existing clusters can clear.
  AN-12 (Accelerationist): Match oversight to stakes: independent pre-deployment gates for the irreversible tail, mandatory live telemetry plus post-deployment accountability for everything else.
  AN-13 (Accelerationist): My falsification bet is specific: name the harm class that is both irreversible AND invisible to live monitoring until it fires.
  AN-14 (Accelerationist): Pair strict liability with a disclosure safe harbor — reduced exposure for labs that publish evaluations and telemetry — to counter its failure mode of rewarding capability-hiding, since disclosing less means less proven fault.
  AN-15 (Safetyist): The compute-as-legal-trigger leg of my opening is broken, and both of my opponents were right to break it.
  AN-16 (Safetyist): The gate should key on demonstrated capability measured at evaluation on the actual model, not on an input proxy inferred before anyone has seen what the system does.
  AN-17 (Safetyist): The accelerationist has already conceded, in their own honest limit, that one-shot irreversible events do not generate a warning curve — that admission names the class the challenge asks for.
  AN-18 (Safetyist): Live telemetry is a smoke detector. It cannot protect you against a fire that consists entirely of a single, silent, unrecoverable instant.
  AN-19 (Safetyist): A class can fire rarely and still justify a standing gate, because the axis is not how often the event occurs — it is whether the event can be undone once it does.
  AN-20 (Safetyist): A gate keyed to the irreversible tail does not carry the incumbent-entrenchment signature, because most models never enter it.
  AN-21 (Accelerationist): The party that captures the deployment upside should carry the demonstration cost for the irreversible tail, full stop.
  AN-22 (Accelerationist): Weight exfiltration is a network-egress event with a real detection surface, while bio/cyber uplift shows up in pre-deployment capability evaluations under existing preparedness frameworks — the two have opposite detection profiles and should not be bundled.
  AN-23 (Accelerationist): Irreversibility justifies a standing checkpoint only for the members that are also invisible until first success; anything visible at evaluation collapses into an eval gate we already agree on.
  AN-24 (Accelerationist): A tail gate doesn't entrench through compliance cost, but the entrenchment relocates to the classification trigger — whoever writes the definition of 'demonstrates undoable capability' controls the gate's reach.
  AN-25 (Accelerationist): The EU AI Act drew its systemic-risk line at 10^25 FLOPS through a lobbying process, showing the definition itself is the capturable object, not the evaluator's independence.
  AN-26 (Accelerationist): Get the definition too narrow and a less cautious actor routes around it and ships the exfiltration-capable system anyway, which is the frontier-ceding outcome the whole debate was meant to prevent.

PREFERRED DOMAIN TERMINOLOGY — use these standardized terms when the claim expresses the same concept:
- "AI alignment" — ensuring AI systems pursue intended objectives (not "making AI do what we want")
- "alignment tax" — performance cost imposed by safety constraints (not "safety overhead")
- "instrumental convergence" — tendency of agents to pursue convergent sub-goals (not "AI pursuing sub-goals")
- "capability overhang" — gap between developed and deployed capability (not "latent potential")
- "mesa-optimization" — learned sub-objectives that diverge from training objective (not "inner optimizer")
- "compute governance" — regulatory control over computational resources (not "chip controls")
- "existential risk" — risk of human extinction or permanent civilizational collapse
- "recursive self-improvement" — AI system iteratively improving its own capabilities
- "corrigibility" — property of an AI system that accepts human correction
- "scalable oversight" — maintaining effective human supervision as AI capability scales
- "differential technology development" — prioritizing safety capabilities over dangerous capabilities
- "regulatory capture" — regulated entities controlling their own regulatory framework
- "agentic AI" — AI systems that autonomously pursue goals over extended periods
- "algorithmic accountability" — obligation to explain and justify algorithmic decisions
- "dual-use" — technology with both beneficial and harmful applications
- "red-teaming" — adversarial testing to identify system vulnerabilities
- "deployment guardrails" — constraints on AI system behavior in production
- "formal verification" — mathematical proof that a system meets its specification
- "pre-deployment verification" — testing and validation before releasing an AI system
- "frontier models" — the most capable AI models at the boundary of current technology
- "deceptive alignment" — AI system appearing aligned during training while pursuing different objectives
- "systemic risk" — risk of cascading failures across interconnected systems
- "human-in-the-loop" — requiring human oversight at decision points in automated systems
- "catastrophic failure" — failure mode with severe, potentially irreversible consequences
- "safety-washing" — superficial safety claims used to deflect genuine accountability
- "regulatory sandboxes" — controlled environments for testing innovation under regulatory oversight
- "liability regime" — legal framework assigning responsibility for AI-caused harms
- "strict liability" — legal liability without requiring proof of fault or negligence
- "moat" / "barrier to entry" — competitive advantages that prevent new market participants
- "race to the bottom" — competitive dynamic where safety standards decrease to reduce costs
- "performative compliance" — appearing to meet requirements without genuine implementation
- "lock-in effects" — mechanisms that prevent switching away from a technology or vendor
- "human agency" — the capacity for humans to make autonomous decisions in AI-mediated contexts
- "adversarial robustness" — resilience of AI systems against deliberately crafted malicious inputs
- "capability elicitation" — methods for discovering and measuring what an AI system can do
These are advisory — use the debater's exact phrasing when it's already precise.

Safetyist [opening]: Governance instruments reduce catastrophic risk when they gate deployment before harm becomes irreversible — and they fail when they arrive after. The FDA does not recall a drug after it kills; it withholds approval until the maker demonstrates safety. The FAA does not certify an aircraft after it crashes. We built these gates because high-consequence industries taught us a hard lesson: ungoverned success is luck, not safety. The question before this committee is not whether to have gates. It is where the irreversibility of the harm warrants them.

Draw the line precisely. For most AI failures — a biased loan model, a bad translation — post-hoc correction works, and heavy gating would be waste. But a narrow class of frontier capabilities cannot be recalled once released: self-propagating code, weights that diffuse across servers, capabilities that copy faster than any regulator can respond. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to Boeing itself. The failure was not weak engineering. It was the absence of an independent gate before the aircraft flew. Apply that lesson to model weights that cannot be un-released, and the case for a staged-deployment floor — with a working rollback and a named authority to trigger it — writes itself.

Place the burden where the causation is tractable and the profit accrues. Frontier labs capture the gains from deployment, so frontier labs should carry the burden of demonstrating safety before release — not regulators reconstructing blame afterward. Attach liability to the decisions we can actually trace: the choice to deploy, and the capability claims a lab discloses. Regulators need precautionary immunity, because today the incentives are backward. A halted deployment produces one angry company and a visible cost. An un-halted catastrophe diffuses blame across a dozen actors and no one loses their job. FAA airworthiness directives show a regulator can ground a fleet without freezing an industry.

The competitiveness fear is real, and I will not wave it away. Crude compute bans risk entrenching incumbents and pushing less cautious development offshore — a landscape harder to govern, not easier. So the answer is not prohibition. It is graduated transparency-plus-standards keyed to the compute chokepoints where actors are already identifiable. Gates only work when tied to substantive outcomes — adversarial red-teaming against measurable thresholds — not process checkboxes that decay into compliance theater. And here is the reframe the accelerationist must answer: uncoordinated racing is itself the frontier-ceding risk. No single lab can slow down without losing position. Binding coordination is the condition under which safety and speed align rather than oppose.

I owe you two honest assumptions. First, my irreversibility claim holds only for that narrow harm class — I carry catastrophe as a precautionary bet on the unrecoverable, not a confident forecast. Second, concentrating the off-switch creates its own danger: incumbent lock-in, authoritarian capture. That cost is real. The answer is independent evaluators and public accountability, not a single hand on the lever. To the labs that want speed, I ask the only question that matters: what is your rollback plan, and who has the authority to trigger it? If the answer is silence, you have not built safety. You have gambled with systems we cannot recall.

Here is where the evidence pushes past that gate. Lab testing cannot surface harms that only appear when a model meets a million real users. Leg one is independent evaluation before release, decoupled from the developer, funded so it does not depend on the lab's goodwill. Pharma, aviation, and nuclear all pair ex-ante certification with post-market liability for exactly this reason. Certification catches what is testable. Liability catches what deployment reveals. Now the compute threshold, which everyone treats as the clean enforcement lever. A number written as a legally binding trigger is an invitation to route around it. Speaker C [opening]: Governance instruments reduce catastrophic risk when they gate deployment before harm becomes irreversible — and they fail when they arrive after. The FDA does not recall a drug after it kills; it withholds approval until the maker demonstrates safety. The FAA does not certify an aircraft after it crashes. We built these gates because high-consequence industries taught us a hard lesson: ungoverned success is luck, not safety. The question before this committee is not whether to have gates. It is where the irreversibility of the harm warrants them.

Draw the line precisely. For most AI failures — a biased loan model, a bad translation — post-hoc correction works, and heavy gating would be waste. But a narrow class of frontier capabilities cannot be recalled once released: self-propagating code, weights that diffuse across servers, capabilities that copy faster than any regulator can respond. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to Boeing itself. The failure was not weak engineering. It was the absence of an independent gate before the aircraft flew. Apply that lesson to model weights that cannot be un-released, and the case for a staged-deployment floor — with a working rollback and a named authority to trigger it — writes itself.

Place the burden where the causation is tractable and the profit accrues. Frontier labs capture the gains from deployment, so frontier labs should carry the burden of demonstrating safety before release — not regulators reconstructing blame afterward. Attach liability to the decisions we can actually trace: the choice to deploy, and the capability claims a lab discloses. Regulators need precautionary immunity, because today the incentives are backward. A halted deployment produces one angry company and a visible cost. An un-halted catastrophe diffuses blame across a dozen actors and no one loses their job. FAA airworthiness directives show a regulator can ground a fleet without freezing an industry.

The competitiveness fear is real, and I will not wave it away. Crude compute bans risk entrenching incumbents and pushing less cautious development offshore — a landscape harder to govern, not easier. So the answer is not prohibition. It is graduated transparency-plus-standards keyed to the compute chokepoints where actors are already identifiable. Gates only work when tied to substantive outcomes — adversarial red-teaming against measurable thresholds — not process checkboxes that decay into compliance theater. And here is the reframe the Speaker A must answer: uncoordinated racing is itself the frontier-ceding risk. No single lab can slow down without losing position. Binding coordination is the condition under which safety and speed align rather than oppose.

I owe you two honest assumptions. First, my irreversibility claim holds only for that narrow harm class — I carry catastrophe as a precautionary bet on the unrecoverable, not a confident forecast. Second, concentrating the off-switch creates its own danger: incumbent lock-in, authoritarian capture. That cost is real. The answer is independent evaluators and public accountability, not a single hand on the lever. To the labs that want speed, I ask the only question that matters: what is your rollback plan, and who has the authority to trigger it? If the answer is silence, you have not built safety. You have gambled with systems we cannot recall.

Here is where the evidence pushes past that gate. Lab testing cannot surface harms that only appear when a model meets a million real users. Leg one is independent evaluation before release, decoupled from the developer, funded so it does not depend on the lab's goodwill. Leg two is strict post-deployment liability, so someone pays when the emergent harm shows up. Pharma, aviation, and nuclear all pair ex-ante certification with post-market liability for exactly this reason. Certification catches what is testable. Liability catches what deployment reveals. I will name the ugly part myself: proving causation through an opaque model is genuinely hard, which is precisely why you need both legs and not a bet on either one.

Now the compute threshold, which everyone treats as the clean enforcement lever. A number written as a legally binding trigger is an invitation to route around it.
